catalog_quote: Apart from the above-mentioned features of the sound system of Sengwer, another aspect of its sound system is the existence of tones in the language. In tonal languages, every syllable is pronounced with a certain melody to it- its tone. Change of tone on a given syllable may change the meaning of the word, be it a mono or polysyllabic word. If a syllable’s tone can modify the meaning of the word. It is called lexical tone. Tones may also have other effects on the language, such as serving grammatical functions. Preliminary data show that Sengwer has two contrastive tones: High and Low and they are generally realized of vowels. A word may have a different lexical meaning depending on whether it is said with a high pitch or a low pitch. world_status: accessible description is silent on stress
sweep_summary: Markweeta (mark1255, Kalenjin/Southern Nilotic; not in the catalog) has exactly one stress-keyword title in this search of works with stress in the title, and it is a Glottolog false positive: Lühr (2004) 'Contrastive Word Stress in Vedic Endo- and Exocentric Compounds' was auto-tagged to Markweeta because of the string 'Endo-' (Glottolog's own reference page says 'computerized assignment from endo'); it is about Vedic Sanskrit, closed access at De Gruyter, priority none. No first-hand word-stress statement for Markweeta was readable in this search of works with stress in the title: the three open papers held by the project (Nandako 2022 on Sengwer; Zwarts 2023, 2024 on Endo-Marakwet) describe the language as a two-tone (H/L) language with lexical and grammatical tone and never mention stress or accent. The one dedicated phonology, Zwarts (2003/2004) 'The Phonology of Endo' (LINCOM 59, 142 pp.), remains print-only (HathiTrust search-only; Harvard offsite copy) and is the high-priority acquisition; Kisang' & Larsen's SIL phonology primer (archive 4957) and Mietzner's 2016 Cherang'any grammar are medium. most external APIs (Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, Google Books, HathiTrust, sil.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The only accessible phonological description of a variety under this languoid (Sengwer = Cherang'any) treats the language as a two-tone (H/L) language with lexical and grammatical tone and makes no statement at all about word stress or accent; the words 'stress' and 'accent' do not occur in the paper. No source opened states where stress falls in Endo/Markweeta proper.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the author flags the tone data as preliminary, from a single speaker.
new_statements.domain_note: Citation-form words from a Swadesh list; word level. The three opened Zwarts papers (2023, 2024) on Endo-Marakwet likewise mention only tone (nominative case and impersonal verbs marked tonally; tone not written in the orthography) and never stress.
new_statements.identity_note: The only opened phonological description (Nandako 2022) is of Sengwer, i.e. Cherang'any/Seng'wer, which Glottolog 5.1 files under mark1255 and which Mietzner and Zwarts treat as a member of the Marakwet cluster distinct from Endo-Marakwet (the northern Marakwet variety that Zwarts 2004/2023/2024 and the BTL Bible describe). Sengwer has no separate glottocode in Glottolog 5.1 (Campbell et al. 2022 list it as 4569-enb under ISO enb). The catalog entry should therefore be tagged as Sengwer/Cherang'any doculect, single-speaker preliminary data, not Endo proper.

Section 5 'Tones' (pp. 8-9): 'Preliminary data show that Sengwer has two contrastive tones: High and Low', lexical (muut 'five' vs 'slow', koi 'liver' vs 'long') and grammatical (number: moi 'calf'/'calves').
